Q: Using PowerShell and wkhtmltopdf to output to PDF A:

tl;dr

Building on your own answer:

Get-ChildItem -Recurse -File -LiteralPath test_input | 
  ForEach-Object { 
    & "wkhtmltopdf.exe" -O landscape --enable-local-file-access $_.FullName "test_output\$($_.BaseName).pdf" 
  }

Note:

  • For conceptual clarity the above uses the ForEach-Object cmdlet's full name in lieu of %, which is one of its built-in aliases.

  • It is only the fact that you've specified the target executable in quotes that syntactically requires its invocation via &, the call operator; without quotes (and in the absence of variable references), & is optional; in other words: & "wkhtmltopdf.exe" could be replaced with just wkhtmltopdf.exe here.

  • -attributes !directory has been replaced with -File to request file-only output, which is more concise and conceptually direct.

  • Since the input path, test_input, contains no wildcard characters, I'm assuming it is to be treated literally (verbatim), in which case the robust choice is to use -LiteralPath rather than -Path, as literal input paths that happen to contain [ / ] would otherwise be misinterpreted; see this answer for more informcation.

Detailed explanation:

I suspect the problem is the \\$_.pdf part

Indeed:

  • Incidentally, using \\ in lieu of \ is unnecessary, but benign: In PowerShell itself, \ has no special meaning and therefore doesn't require escaping. However, using verbatim \\ as a path separator is generally quietly tolerated.

  • Crucially, however, $_ contains the full path of the input file at hand, due to the preceding % { $_.fullname } pipeline segment, whereas your intent was for $_ refer to the base name, i.e. the mere file name of the input without its extension.

I've tried a bunch of different properties on the $_ object, and length is the only one that has substituted a value, so I have no idea what's going on.

  • % { $_.fullname } (% being a built-in alias of the built-in ForEach-Object cmdlet) emits the full path of each input file as a string, i.e. an instance of [string], whose only (.NET type-native) property is .Length

  • In PowerShell - by default - any attempt to reference a nonexistent property quietly results in $null being returned.

    • In the context of string interpolation, i.e. inside an expandable (interpolating) string (double-quoted, i.e. "..."), $null simply becomes the empty string, i.e. doesn't contribute any characters to the resulting string, which explains the outcome of your attempt to use an (imagined) .namestring property.

    • Via Set-StrictMode -Version 2 or above, you could instruct PowerShell to report errors in response to attempts to access nonexistent properties, but that comes with pitfalls - see this answer.

Therefore:

  • Do not use % { $_.fullname }, as it prevents you from (easily) deriving the base file name from each input file in subsequent pipeline segments.

  • Using the input file objects emitted by Get-ChildItem - which are of type System.IO.FileInfo - as-is, allows you to conveniently reference the base file name as $_.BaseName

    • Inside "..." - as shown in your own answer - referencing $_.BaseName requires enclosure in $(...), for syntactic reasons explained in this answer.

Q: Powershell Move-Item fails to move contents of current directory to new subdirectory A:

Theo has provided the crucial pointer:

  • The -Path (-FilePath) parameter of provider cmdlets (which the first positional argument implicitly binds to), expects wildcard expressions.

    • Because PowerShell's wildcard language also supports expressions such as [a-z] (to match any English letter), paths meant to be literal ones are misinterpreted if they happen to contain [ chars.

      • To pass a literal (verbatim) path as such, use the -LiteralPath parameter explicitly.

      • Alternatively, pass a file-information object such as produced by Get-ChildItem via the pipeline to a provider cmdlet, which also binds to
        -LiteralPath

    • For more information, see this answer.

  • Additionally, it is simpler to use the -Force switch with New-Item -ItemType Directory to ensure on-demand creation of a directory path, which obviates the need for a
    Test-Path call.

    • Specifically, -Force creates any missing components of the specified directory path, if needed, and takes no action if the path already exists in full.
    • In either case, a [System.IO.DirectoryInfo] instance describing the newly created or preexisting directory is output.

To put it all together in the context of your code, with additional optimizations applied:

# ... 

$mainDir = 'E:\scripttest'
# -Directory limits the output to subdirectories.
Get-ChildItem -Directory -LiteralPath $mainDir |
  ForEach-Object {
    # Extract the author's name and the remaining part of the directory name
    if ($_.Name -match '^(.*?) - (.*)$') {
      $author = $matches[1]
      $title = $matches[2]
      # Ensure that the target dir. exists, using -Force.
      $newSubDir = New-Item -Force -ItemType Directory -Path (
        Join-Path (Join-Path $mainDir $author) $title
      )
      # Move all files in the input dir. to the destination dir.
      # Note the use of the pipeline, which implicitly ensures 
      # binding to the -LiteralPath parameter while also being more
      # efficient than calling Move-Item in a ForEach-Object loop. 
      $_ | Get-ChildItem -File | Move-Item -Destination $newSubDir -Force
    }
  }

Note:

  • With New-Item, the -Path parameter is used, which effectively functions like -LiteralPath (which this cmdlet doesn't technically support).

Q: How is the way to write 3D Web Application for Custom Tailoring? A:

The tailor application you gave a link you uses quite low-tech approach. It uses (pre?)generated images for each option (using transparency layer). Images are stacked one upon another to produce the final result.

Of course, the end-result is looking nice, which is due to careful web-design.

In short: you need a pile of carefully prepared images (it's a lot of routine work unless you have them readily 3d-modelled) for each detail and clever URL-mapping to choose the image. Everything else is just programming choices in HTML/javascript and loading correct images into corresponding layers.

Use browser's development tools (like Firebug for Firefox) to discover how the application works.
